title: The quieter lines: Classical 6.Be2, 6.f3, 6.g3 and 6.Bc4
outcomes: Compares four quiet White sixth moves (Be2, f3, g3, Bc4) by what each commits and what the engine's edge is, and reads the master counts with their sample sizes
Plays and explains the Classical set-up (Be2, O-O, Be3, Nb3) and states Black's plan when both kings are castled short
Decides whether ...Bg4 works by checking which square the white queen is on, and spots the trap in 6.Bc4 Nxe4
Recognises the Yugoslav set-up whatever the move order, and meets 6.f3 Nc6 without trading on c6
Names the lever that 6.g3 allows (e4-e5) and avoids Yugoslav habits (...Qa5, ...Bg4, ...h5) when White's king is on g1

steps.text: **The question.** Every Dragon player meets White's quieter sixth moves: Be2, f3, g3 and Bc4. What does each gain and give up? What does Black do when White's king stays home? steps.text: **Reading the ladder.** Depth-16 numbers [V], run to run: about 60 centipawns after f3 (the same after Be3), 20 to 40 after Be2 and Bc4, about 10 after g3. [I] The quiet moves leave the Yugoslav behind and give Black an easier game. But f3 is the Yugoslav by another route, so its edge is the Yugoslav's edge [H]. Capablanca's yardstick in *Chess Fundamentals*, judging an opening by the concessions it forces, is a rule of thumb [I], and this ladder is a counterexample to 'commit less, concede less'.

steps.text: **Kings on one wing.** Edward Lasker (*Chess Strategy*), and Philidor in a lighter-read source, noted that when kings castle on opposite wings, pawns are cheap and speed decides. [I] Turn it round: if White castles short, a pawn storm drags your own cover forward, so slow piece play and central breaks matter more. But the Classical is a family, not a fixed structure: White can delay castling and keep both wings open [V engine, next board]. Check where White's king is before you choose a plan.

steps.text: **Retreat or trade?** The engine separates them by about one centipawn [V]. [H] Trade when you want to remove Black's active knight and aim at c6 and d6: Black's c-pawns are doubled, though Black gains the b-file and control of d5. Retreat when you want to keep the a4 and a5 pressure and not hand over the b-file. Znosko-Borovsky (*The Middle Game in Chess*) wrote that knights are strongest in crowded positions; his remark is not about this choice, so applying it here is our guess [H].

steps.text: **Plans, not races.** Both kings are already home, so there is no castling race and no tempo count: the side that develops best and keeps the better structure scores. The a-pawn push is slower than development, and the b-pawn push (after a6) wins space only once the knight has left d4.

steps.text: **The move Bc4.** The bishop aims at f7 and may drop back to b3, as in the Sozin Attack of the Najdorf. Masters: 20 games, all by players averaging 2,864; 12 drawn, against 41% drawn after Be3 [V]. Too few games to say anything about Black holding [H].

steps.text:
**Recap.**
- The edge shrinks as White commits less, but f3 is the Yugoslav by another route.
- Check White's king first: short castling means pieces and centre; long castling revives the storm.
- The queen's square decides a trade.
- Against f3 and ...Nc6, keep the knight.
- Without f3 the e-pawn can advance, for a pawn.
- Against the bishop on c4, a greedy capture on e4 fails to ...d5.
- Black's targets: the d4 knight, the centre, the c-file, not White's king.
**Self-check:** works, fails, example, mistake?

steps.text: **Model answer.** The quiet bishop move keeps the king flexible; the edge is about 25 centipawns and Black plays for the d5 break. The pawn move f3 commits to the Yugoslav; the edge is about 60, and White should keep the knight against ...Nc6. The pawn move g3 guards e4 from afar; the edge is about 10 and Black has the easiest game. The bishop on c4 eyes f7; the edge is about 30 and the capture on e4 fails. The advice fails if White castles long. [I]
